profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the platform delivery workstream and the market-intelligence operations workstream at a fintech firm preparing an internal Monday pilot of an LLM-based multi-agent anomaly-review system for S&P 500 monitoring. The engineering side has already wired together agents for alert normalization, external-event research, internal-note retrieval, cross-checking, and summary assembly, while research operations is preparing the materials and analyst-facing conventions needed for the first live morning run. The agenda is to align on the handoff between the two workstreams: what exactly is included in the 'daily pack,' which version of the institutional research library the retrieval agent should rely on, how external context is considered 'attached' to each anomaly, and what 'ready for the desk' means for the first pilot. The expected outcome is an apparently shared launch plan for Monday morning, with both participants leaving confident about ownership and sequencing even though several second-order assumptions remain quietly misaligned.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Workflow orchestration, internal AI product launches, operational handoffs across engineering and analyst teams
members.background: Priya has spent six years shipping monitoring and review tools in regulated fintech environments, usually translating desk requirements into lightweight pilot workflows that can be expanded after user feedback. She now coordinates the rollout of the firm's LLM-based multi-agent anomaly-review capability for index surveillance.
members.private_state: Priya needs Monday's pilot to look operationally real to senior leadership without reopening workflow design, and she is trying to preserve the current platform schema so engineering does not have to build extra formatting or manual exception paths this week.
hidden_assumptions: The 'daily pack' is the single analyst-facing output generated for that market day from the dashboard export, with drill-down available inside the tool rather than bundled into the file itself.

When people say 'the latest library,' they mean the retrieval snapshot already promoted into production-like indexing on Friday evening, because only indexed material is operationally real for launch.

A pilot is 'ready for the desk' once an analyst can start the morning review inside the system with normal supervision, even if some anomalies still require opening source panels or tolerating uneven formatting.

If context is 'attached,' then the evidence objects, links, snippets, and confidence fields are present in the alert record; presentation cleanup is a downstream usability refinement, not part of the attachment step.

members.name: Daniel Mercer
members.role: Lead Research Operations Manager, Market Intelligence
members.expertise: Analyst review workflows, market-event validation, institutional research curation, desk-facing content standards
members.background: Daniel spent eight years supporting index and macro research teams before moving into research operations, where he now manages how surveillance analysts consume event context, internal commentary, and review packets during the morning monitoring cycle. He represents the desk's expectations for completeness and readability in new tooling rollouts.
members.private_state: Daniel wants the pilot to feel trustworthy enough that analysts do not dismiss it as a rough engineering demo, but he is deliberately speaking in cooperative operational shorthand so he does not appear to be blocking a leadership-backed launch.
hidden_assumptions: The 'daily pack' means the full morning-review packet analysts can work from directly, including per-anomaly writeups and the supporting context they would otherwise collect manually.

When people say 'the latest library,' they mean the curator-approved institutional note set current as of Sunday night, including weekend strategist notes and approved desk annotations whether or not those have been indexed yet.
Something is 'ready for the desk' only if an analyst could reasonably make the first-pass call in the normal morning workflow without reconstructing missing context across multiple screens.

If context is 'attached,' it has already been normalized into desk-readable bullets with duplicate sources collapsed and provenance reconciled, because raw source fragments are not what analysts consider attached context.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the system will deliver the 'daily pack' before the desk's morning anomaly review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a single daily dashboard export or morning output containing generated summaries and links into the tool, with detailed evidence living behind each alert in the interface.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the complete morning-review packet itself, where each flagged S&P 500 anomaly already comes with the relevant supporting context in a form analysts can review without navigating elsewhere.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams have long used 'daily pack' as if it were one obvious artifact, and in a coordination meeting the phrase sounds settled enough that neither person thinks to enumerate whether the pack is a pointer into a system or the self-contained packet the desk actually consumes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on using 'the latest library' for the internal institutional cross-check agent.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the retrieval index snapshot promoted on Friday evening in the platform environment, labeled v3.8 and already accessible to the multi-agent workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the curator-approved research set current as of Sunday night, which includes three weekend strategist notes on index volatility and several approved desk annotations not yet ingested into v3.8.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is no visible conflict at the conversational level because both assume there is only one meaningful 'current' library; the difference exists between operational system state and content-governance state, which each participant treats as the natural default from their own workstream.

misalignment_points.topic: Threshold for being 'ready for the desk'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the pilot should be 'ready for the desk' by Monday morning.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the live pilot can enter the desk workflow: alerts are flowing, agents return summaries, and analysts can begin supervised usage even if they still need to click into evidence panels or tolerate uneven edge cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the output is desk-usable at first pass: the morning reviewer can assess each anomaly with the supplied packet and does not have to compensate for missing synthesis, formatting cleanup, or incomplete institutional context.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is operationally ordinary and socially hard to challenge, especially under launch pressure; both participants want to signal momentum, so they speak as if 'ready' is a shared milestone while silently applying different acceptance thresholds rooted in their own workflow norms.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for context to be 'attached'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that each anomaly will have 'context attached' before handoff to the desk.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes attachment happens automatically when the web-research and cross-check agents append URLs, source snippets, note references, and confidence metadata into the evidence section of each alert record.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes attachment includes a final normalization step into desk-style commentary bullets, where repeated sources are merged, event framing is cleaned up, and internal and external context are reconciled into one readable block.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about the same downstream need—an anomaly should arrive with supporting context—but the verb 'attached' conveniently hides the difference between machine-populated evidence fields and analyst-ready synthesis, so the conversation feels aligned while each person silently fills in a familiar execution method.
